children: Revenue per employee (RPE) rose sequentially across India’s top five IT services companies in Q2 FY27. However, rising subcontracting, AI-led automation and pricing pressures are challenging the relevance of the traditional productivity metric.

According to UnearthInsight data, revenue per FTE increased sequentially, with Tech Mahindra recording the sharpest growth at 7.1 per cent to $11,123, alongside a 0.3 per cent decline in headcount. The company’s performance coincided with a twelfth consecutive quarter of margin expansion under Project Fortius.

TCS reported a 1.5 per cent  quarter-on-quarter increase in revenue per FTE to $12,778, even as its headcount grew 0.8 per cent. Infosys recorded a 1.2 per cent rise to $15,472, with headcount remaining flat.
Wipro’s revenue per FTE increased 0.7 per cent to $10,930, while its workforce grew 0.4 per cent. HCLTech saw a 0.6 per cent increase to $16,167, despite a 1.6 per cent rise in headcount.
Gaurav Vasu, CEO and Founder of UnearthInsight, explained that RPE was designed for a business where people did all the work — a model that is evolving.

He explained that when a share of delivery comes from AI agents, subcontractors, and partner platforms, dividing revenue by headcount tells less about productivity. Instead, the industry needs to move to a set of measures rather than one ratio — revenue per billable delivery employee rather than total headcount. The second is revenue per unit of total delivery cost, combining employee costs, subcontracting spend, and AI compute and licensing costs. The third is mix-adjusted measurement.

Saravanan Balasundaram, Founder and CEO of Han Digital Group, shared that at India’s largest IT services firm, spend on external consultants rose more than 35 per cent and on software and infrastructure about 30 per cent in a year, while payroll stayed flat in dollar terms.
Since contractors do not appear in headcount, a company can show higher RPE simply by moving work to them.
Biswajeet Mahapatra, Principal Analyst, Forrester, echoed this, noting that subcontracted capacity can support delivery without appearing in the employee denominator.

“Greater reliance on subcontractors can support RPE even though the underlying cost of delivering that revenue may be increasing. Benchmark research shows that contracted technology talent can carry a premium in several environments, including an average annual cost of $152,700 for contracted public-cloud FTEs versus $135,000 for employees. Subcontracting may make employee-based productivity metrics look better, while simultaneously putting pressure on delivery economics if expensive external capacity is being used to fill scarce skills or meet variable demand,” he said.

On the other hand, Balasundaram added that the industry must move from RPE to revenue per unit of delivery capacity, counting human FTEs together with the agentic capacity paid for through compute, licences and platforms.

“Three companion metrics should sit alongside it: gross profit per employee, AI revenue per AI-skilled professional, and constant-currency RPE, since rupee depreciation alone added nearly 9 per cent to rupee-reported RPE between Q2 FY26 and Q2 FY27. Agents should be counted as capacity, not hidden as cost. The talent model isn’t going away, but is being repriced,” he said.

Vasu shared that over time, leading firms may report agent capacity — tasks or hours handled by agents- and to link revenue to outcomes delivered rather than effort. Until then, RPE figures should be read alongside margins, utilisation and subcontracting trends,” Vasu said.

Moreover, while AI productivity is real at the delivery level, little has turned into higher RPE. The reason is pricing. Clients that have put AI into production now expect the efficiency gains to show up in their contracts. This pass-through is happening mainly at renewal of large multi-year deals, and industry estimates put the resulting deflation on traditional services revenue at around 2 per cent to 3 per cent a year.

Siddhartha Tipnis, Partner and Technology Sector Leader, Deloitte India, noted that in FY26, Tier-1 IT/ITeS firms delivered low-single-digit revenue growth alongside a net headcount contraction of approximately 7,000 FTEs, driving 3–4 per cent RPE growth largely through workforce rationalisation. In H1 FY27, hiring resumed, with net headcount additions of approximately 16,000 FTEs across Tier 1 firms, while  dollar revenue growth at the four largest firms remained subdued at 0.7–2.6 per cent.

The underlying challenge is that AI productivity gains are increasingly being passed on to clients through pricing and delivery efficiencies. This enables enterprises to meet existing demand at lower cost, rather than unlocking incremental AI spending or creating new revenue pools. Greater subcontracting and favourable foreign-exchange movements provide some offset, but do not fundamentally resolve the pressure on underlying productivity economics.

The next phase of value creation will depend not merely on generating AI-driven productivity, but on converting it into incremental demand, differentiated offerings and sustainable revenue growth without proportional headcount expansion.

“We estimate that RPE in AI-integrated operations could be 10 per cent to 15 per cent higher. Until AI makes up a much larger share of revenue, and pricing moves from effort-based to outcome-based models, most of the benefit will go to clients rather than show up in RPE,” according to Vasu.

Praveen Bhadada, CEO and Managing Director of Neovay Global, said revenue growth remains subdued despite rising RPE, as AI-led productivity gains are largely passed on to clients through lower pricing. With AI still accounting for a small share of IT services revenue and often replacing existing work rather than creating new demand, meaningful RPE growth will depend on a shift from effort-based to outcome-based pricing. Until then, AI is more likely to protect margins than drive revenue growth.

title: AI challenges traditional productivity metrics for Indian IT
